historical_timeline.summary: Her father's lupus diagnosed after an illness first thought to be rheumatoid arthritis.
Her father died of systemic lupus erythematosus.
Month-long hospital stay in Georgia with an operation for a floating kidney.

claims.statement: Mary Flannery O'Connor was born in Savannah, Georgia, on March 25, 1925, the only child of Edward Francis O'Connor and Regina Cline O'Connor. She later dropped her first name for her writing.

Her father was diagnosed with lupus in 1937; his illness began with a whitish patch of skin on his forehead and arthritis, and was first diagnosed as rheumatoid arthritis. He died of systemic lupus erythematosus in 1941, a month after his 45th birthday, when she was 15.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented family history of systemic lupus erythematosus in a first-degree relative.

claims.statement: O'Connor graduated from Georgia State College for Women in 1945 and then studied at the Writers' Workshop of the State University of Iowa, where she earned a Master of Fine Arts; she was writing her first novel by the late 1940s.
In December 1949, at 24, she fell seriously ill on a holiday visit to Georgia and spent about a month in hospital, where she had an operation for a floating kidney.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A physician friend later speculated that this was the first sign of lupus; a review in a medical society journal notes that lupus nephritis is usually painless, so whether it was is unclear.

source_links.locator: A 1949 operation to correct a floating kidney

claims.statement: In 1950, while living in Connecticut and writing Wise Blood, O'Connor developed joint pain; rheumatoid arthritis was suspected, a diagnosis that later proved wrong.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented presentation that the synthetic episode echoes; the month of onset is not given.

claims.statement: In December 1950 she traveled home to Georgia by train and arrived looking very ill. She was admitted to hospital in Milledgeville, kidney disease was suspected, and on the advice of an Atlanta kidney specialist who suspected lupus she was moved to Emory Hospital in Atlanta, where a positive LE cell test confirmed systemic lupus erythematosus.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Sources date the diagnosis to late 1950 or January 1951; it was made in Atlanta.

source_links.locator: Doctors in Atlanta diagnosed her condition as lupus

claims.statement: Fearing the shock of her having the disease that had killed her father, her mother chose not to tell her the diagnosis; O'Connor learned that she had lupus from a friend in mid-1951.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented nondisclosure within the family; the synthetic episode tells her the diagnosis directly. No decision in the modern episode is attributed to any relative.

claims.statement: She was discharged on daily injections of ACTH, which she learned to give herself, and was later treated with cortisone and prednisone. In early 1953 she wrote that she was nearly bald on top and had a "watermelon face".
claims.clinical_interpretation: Hair loss and a round face are taken by the medical authors as signs of steroid treatment (iatrogenic Cushing syndrome).

claims.statement: From 1951 until 1964 O'Connor lived with her mother at Andalusia, the family farm outside Milledgeville, Georgia, where she wrote and kept peafowl and other birds.

By the spring of 1954 she had a limp and progressive hip pain, and she used crutches for most of her remaining years. She later wrote that her doctors had found that her "bone disintegration is being caused by the steroid drugs" she had taken for years.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her own report of her physicians' finding, as quoted in a medical society journal.

claims.statement: Physician authors attribute her hip disease to avascular necrosis of the femoral head from steroid treatment, and suggest that her jaw may have been affected in the same way.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective medical interpretation from her letters and photographs; no imaging from her lifetime was reviewed.

claims.statement: Physician authors suggest from her letters and photographs that she may have had a malar facial rash early in her illness and the hand deformities of Jaccoud arthropathy.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; not used as a historical finding.

claims.statement: Her steroid treatment was tapered in the first half of 1961, when she was also taking chloroquine.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Later than the synthetic episode and not used in it.

claims.statement: In early 1964 she was anemic from a bleeding fibroid tumor and had abdominal surgery to remove it; the tumor was benign, but the operation reactivated her lupus, which had been in remission, and her kidneys were affected.
claims.clinical_interpretation: One source describes the operation as a hysterectomy. Later than the synthetic episode and not used in it.

claims.statement: Her novel Wise Blood was published in 1952 and A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories in 1955; The Complete Stories won the National Book Award after her death.
O'Connor died of kidney failure from lupus in the Baldwin County Hospital in Milledgeville on August 3, 1964, at 39.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without detail.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize systemic lupus erythematosus in a woman of 25 with inflammatory arthritis, fever, a malar rash, cytopenias, and protein and blood in the urine, rather than calling it rheumatoid arthritis; classify it with the 1943 EULAR/ACR criteria (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, complements, antiphospholipid antibodies) and tell her the diagnosis directly. Measure the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, biopsy the kidney, and treat class III lupus nephritis as the 1948 ACR and 1947 EULAR guidance advise: hydroxychloroquine for every patient with baseline eye screening, pulse then tapering glucocorticoids kept to 5 mg a day or less, mycophenolate with belimumab, and an angiotensin receptor blocker. Protect bone and watch for avascular necrosis, give vaccinations before immunosuppression, protect her from the sun, manage cardiovascular risk, plan contraception and any future pregnancy with her antiphospholipid status in mind, and protect her writing life. The teaching note contrasts this with the high-dose steroid treatment, the steroid bone damage, and the concealment of her diagnosis that she lived through.

hpi.narrative: Ms. O'Connor returns nine days after presenting with three months of painful, swollen hands, wrists, and knees, evening fevers, fatigue, a facial rash after sun, and protein and blood in her urine. She saw Dr. Okonjo-Strand this morning, and the tests drawn there returned this afternoon: ANA positive at 1:640 in a homogeneous pattern, anti-dsDNA 186 IU/mL, anti-Sm 42 U/mL, and low complements (C3 62, C4 8 mg/dL). Anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies are negative and the lupus anticoagulant test is negative. The urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 1.8 g/g, with 22 red cells per high-power field, many of them misshapen, and a red cell cast; creatinine is 0.8. Hepatitis B surface antigen is negative with a positive surface antibody, and hepatitis C and HIV tests are negative; a pregnancy test is negative. Before the results were given she was asked how she wanted to hear them and said she wanted all of it, at once. She was told directly that she has systemic lupus erythematosus, that the urine findings mean the kidneys are probably involved, and that a kidney biopsy is needed to choose treatment; she knows that her father had lupus, and was told plainly that treatment and outlook today are very different. She repeated it back accurately. She asked that her diagnosis not be shared with anyone she has not named.

hpi.narrative: Ms. O'Connor is thirteen weeks into treatment. Her joint pain and swelling settled within three weeks and the facial rash has faded with sun protection; she has had no fevers. She takes prednisone 10 mg a day, reached a month ago, mycophenolate 1000 mg twice daily (loose stools in the first two weeks, since settled), weekly belimumab by her own injection, hydroxychloroquine, and losartan. She has gained 3.4 kg and sleeps less well on the days after a dose reduction. She writes five mornings a week.

assessment.assessment: ANA 1:640 meets the EULAR/ACR entry criterion, and the weighted criteria score 32 (fever, thrombocytopenia, acute cutaneous lupus, joint involvement, proteinuria, low C3 and C4, anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm), so she is classified as having lupus; anti-dsDNA 186 and anti-Sm 42 are highly specific. Disease activity is high (SLEDAI-2K 23). The arthritis of lupus mimics rheumatoid arthritis, which is why it is often misnamed. Antiphospholipid antibodies and lupus anticoagulant are negative

A protein-to-creatinine ratio of 1.8 g/g with dysmorphic red cells and a red cell cast and normal creatinine almost certainly means lupus nephritis. A kidney biopsy is needed now, because the class decides treatment

Hydroxychloroquine for every patient with lupus, at 5 mg/kg or less, now. If the biopsy shows class III or IV nephritis: three days of pulse methylprednisolone, then prednisone from about 0.5 mg/kg tapered to 5 mg a day or less by six months, with mycophenolate 2 to 3 g a day plus a second agent, either belimumab or a calcineurin inhibitor such as voclosporin, continued for years after a complete response. An angiotensin receptor blocker for proteinuria and blood pressure. If the class were V alone, the plan would change

Non-live vaccines are best given before immunosuppression: PCV20 and recombinant zoster can be given today and influenza was given in October. She is immune to hepatitis B by vaccination and negative for hepatitis C and HIV. Pneumocystis prophylaxis can be considered while the prednisone dose is high; sulfonamides are best avoided in lupus

Mycophenolate causes birth defects and needs highly effective contraception. With negative antiphospholipid tests, estrogen is not contraindicated by clotting risk, but an intrauterine system is the most effective choice during active disease. Pregnancy should wait for at least six months of quiet disease on compatible medicines

High-dose glucocorticoids threaten bone and can cause avascular necrosis of the hip, especially at high doses. A DXA at the start, vitamin D and calcium, and the lowest glucocorticoid dose protect her; new hip, groin, or knee pain needs prompt MRI. Hydroxychloroquine needs a baseline eye examination with OCT and visual fields within the first year

Lupus clusters in families, and first-degree relatives have a much higher relative risk, although the absolute risk to any one relative is low. No genetic test is needed. She was told that treatment and outcomes today are very different from those of earlier generations
